learn.title: Rooftop Solar and Net Metering in India
learn.intro: Rooftop solar turns homes, schools and factories into mini power stations, slashing electricity bills and grid demand. India's net metering policy lets prosumers export surplus power and earn credits, making clean energy adoption both practical and profitable nationwide.
learn.c1_text: Photovoltaic panels mounted on your roof convert sunlight into direct current electricity. An inverter then changes this DC into alternating current that powers your appliances. Surplus energy flows back to the grid whenever your generation exceeds consumption, turning every sunny rooftop into a power plant.
learn.c2_text: A bidirectional net meter tracks units you import from and export to the grid. At month end, exported units are deducted from imported units, so you only pay the net difference. Some states also compensate surplus exports through feed-in tariffs or banking arrangements for nighttime use.
learn.c3_text: The PM-Surya Ghar Yojana targets 1 crore households with 300 units of free monthly electricity. MNRE offers central subsidies up to Rs 78,000 for residential systems under 3 kW. India aims for 40 GW of rooftop solar capacity by 2026 through state-level net metering frameworks.
learn.stat1: India installed over 4.5 GW of rooftop solar by 2024
learn.stat2: PM-Surya Ghar scheme targets 1 crore rooftop installations
learn.stat3: Central subsidy up to Rs 78,000 for 2 kW systems
learn.stat4: National target: 40 GW rooftop solar by 2026

learn.title: How Solar PV Panels Generate Electricity
learn.intro: Solar panels silently convert sunlight into electricity with no moving parts, fuel, or emissions. Understanding the photoelectric effect reveals how photons knock electrons free, enabling clean power generation that has grown into the world's fastest-expanding energy source.
learn.c1_text: When photons strike silicon cells, they transfer energy to electrons in the atomic lattice. If the photon carries enough energy, it ejects the electron from its bond. A built-in electric field at the p-n junction then drives these freed electrons in one direction, creating direct current electricity.
learn.c2_text: A typical crystalline silicon cell has two silicon layers doped with phosphorus and boron, creating a permanent electric field at their junction. Antireflective coatings and metal contacts capture more light and channel electrons outward. Most modern cells convert 20 to 22 percent of incident sunlight into usable electricity.
learn.c3_text: India's Bhadla Solar Park in Rajasthan spans 14,000 acres across 5,700 hectares with 2.25 GW capacity. Sixty to seventy-two cells form a panel, panels combine into strings, and strings feed inverters that synchronize with India's grid. A single large park can power over a million homes cleanly.
learn.stat1: Modern silicon solar cells reach 22 percent efficiency
learn.stat2: Bhadla Solar Park capacity: 2.25 GW in Rajasthan

learn.stat4: Global solar PV capacity crossed 1.6 TW in 2024

learn.title: Offshore Wind Farms: Design and Grid Connection
learn.intro: Offshore wind farms harness stronger, steadier winds over open seas, delivering large-scale clean power to coastal megacities. They are central to deep decarbonization but demand sophisticated engineering, floating platforms, and undersea transmission to connect remote turbines to onshore grids.
learn.c1_text: Modern offshore turbines stand over 260 metres tall with rotor diameters exceeding 220 metres. Fixed-bottom monopile foundations suit waters under 60 metres, while floating semisubmersible platforms with mooring lines unlock the 80 percent of offshore potential in deeper seas.
learn.c2_title: Fixed-bottom foundations work up to 60 m water depth
learn.c2_text: Inter-array cables link turbines within the farm, while an export cable carries aggregated power to an onshore substation. High-voltage AC is used for distances under 80 kilometres; beyond that, HVDC converter stations minimize transmission losses across the long subsea journey.
learn.c3_text: India has identified potential for 175 GW of offshore wind capacity along its 7,600 kilometre coastline. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has allocated initial project sites off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, with a target of 30 GW by 2030 supported by viability gap funding and seabed leasing reforms.
learn.stat1: Largest offshore turbines exceed 15 MW capacity each
learn.stat3: India's coastline length: 7,600 km with massive wind potential
learn.stat4: India targets 30 GW offshore wind capacity by 2030

learn.title: PLI Scheme for Solar Manufacturing in India
learn.intro: India's Production Linked Incentive scheme is rebuilding domestic solar manufacturing from scratch, reducing costly import dependence. By paying manufacturers per unit produced, PLI accelerates gigawatt-scale factories, creates skilled jobs, and strengthens supply chain resilience in the global clean energy race.
learn.c1_text: Under the PLI scheme, the government pays manufacturers a fixed incentive for every additional unit of solar modules or cells produced above a baseline. The Rs 19,500 crore allocation rewards incremental production, encouraging firms to expand capacity, localize supply chains, and scale up operations rapidly.
learn.c2_title: Vertical Integration of Solar Supply Chain 🔗
learn.c2_text: The scheme covers polysilicon, ingots, wafers, cells, and modules, encouraging manufacturers to control multiple stages. Vedanta, Adani, Reliance, and Tata have committed over Rs 50,000 crore in integrated manufacturing. Vertical integration reduces raw material risks and improves quality control across the production process.
learn.c3_text: India's earlier reliance on Chinese solar imports created strategic vulnerabilities after 2022 border tensions. The PLI is expected to add 48,337 MW of domestic module manufacturing capacity and 38,000 MW of cell capacity, supporting the 500 GW non-fossil target while generating 1.95 lakh direct jobs.
learn.stat1: PLI allocation: Rs 19,500 crore for solar manufacturing

learn.title: Perovskite Solar Cells: Next Generation Efficiency
learn.intro: Perovskite solar cells promise to shatter silicon's dominance by offering high efficiency at a fraction of the cost. These lightweight, printable materials can be coated on flexible surfaces, opening possibilities from windows to backpacks, and could redefine how humanity harvests sunlight.
learn.c1_text: Perovskites are a class of materials with a specific ABX3 crystal structure. Methylammonium lead iodide is the most studied solar perovskite, absorbing light up to 10 times more strongly than silicon per unit thickness. They can be solution-processed, inkjet-printed, or roll-to-roll manufactured at very low temperatures.
learn.c2_text: Single-junction perovskite cells have reached over 26 percent efficiency in laboratory settings, up from just 4 percent in 2009. Tandem stacks pairing perovskite on silicon have crossed 33 percent, surpassing the 29.4 percent theoretical Shockley-Queisser limit for single-junction silicon cells by a significant margin.
learn.c3_text: Researchers are stacking perovskite layers on silicon cells to capture broader light spectra, pushing tandem efficiency above 33 percent. India's National Solar Energy Federation and IIT Bombay are working on lead-free and moisture-resistant formulations. Stability under heat, humidity, and light remains the key commercialization barrier.
learn.stat3: Light absorption: 10 times stronger than silicon per micron
learn.stat4: Efficiency growth: from 4 percent in 2009 to 26 percent by 2024

learn.title: India National Green Hydrogen Mission Explained
learn.intro: Green hydrogen, produced by splitting water with renewable electricity, is set to decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors like steel, fertilizer, and heavy transport. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission aims to make the country a global hub, cutting imports and enabling deep industrial decarbonization.
learn.c1_text: Green hydrogen is produced through electrolysis powered entirely by renewable energy. An electrolyzer passes current through water, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen without emissions. Unlike grey hydrogen from natural gas, green hydrogen produces zero carbon during production, making it a clean fuel and industrial feedstock.
learn.c2_text: The mission targets 5 million metric tonnes of annual green hydrogen production by 2030, supported by about 125 GW of dedicated renewable energy capacity. It also seeks to attract Rs 8 lakh crore in cumulative investments and create over 6 lakh jobs across the emerging hydrogen value chain ecosystem nationwide.
learn.c3_text: The mission offers Rs 17,490 crore in incentives for electrolyzer manufacturing, green hydrogen production, and pilot projects in steel and mobility. Bidders like Reliance, Adani, and L&T are setting up gigawatt-scale electrolyzer plants. Green ammonia exports to Europe and Japan form a key early demand driver.
learn.stat1: Production target: 5 MMT per year by 2030
learn.stat3: Target investment: Rs 8 lakh crore cumulative
learn.stat4: Expected employment generation: 6 lakh jobs by 2030
